section: 1.  Identify the most-recent date tag among saved CSVs
start_anchor: all_csv   <- list.files(results_dir, pattern = file_regex, full.names = TRUE)
grain_in: one CSV file on disk in results/ whose name matches the date-stamped pattern
grain_out: one row per base name, i.e. one chosen file per result family
operation: Lists files in results/ matching the nine base names plus a _YYYY-MM-DD suffix, parses base and date out of each filename, refilters to base_names, sorts by base then date descending then filename descending, and keeps the first row per base so downstream work always uses the newest stamp; the missing-base setdiff and warning are absorbed because they only report on the selection just made. The base names in the code (portfolio_ps, L5_alpha_diversity_observed, beta_bray_pairs_monthly, beta_bray_bay_period_season) disagree with those listed in the file header comment (portfolio_effect, L5_alpha_diversity, beta_bray_consecutive_years); the code is what runs.
settings: Regex ^(base|...)_\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}\.csv$ anchored at both ends; recency judged from the date in the filename, not file modification time; tie-break arrange(base, desc(date), desc(fname)) then slice_head(n = 1); nine base names hard-coded; results_dir fixed to script_dir/results.
na_behavior: A base with no matching file yields no row at all rather than an NA row; the check issues a warning and execution continues, so the failure surfaces later as an object-not-found error at the rename step. A file whose date is malformed fails the regex and is invisible here, indistinguishable from a file that does not exist.
notes: Standard filing convention I developed. Used in other code as well.

section: 2. Read each latest file into a named list
grain_out: one data frame per base; most are one row per major_area x period x season, but what one row of beta_bray_pairs_monthly or beta_bray_bay_period_season represents cannot be determined from this script
units_out: mixed across tables: species counts, diversity indices, invariability indices, dissimilarities
operation: Reads each selected CSV, deframes to a named list, pushes the list into the global environment, and aliases the long table names to the short ones used downstream. The aliases are absorbed because they only carry a table forward, but the region deliberately includes them so a reviewer can see which file becomes alpha_div, gamma_div and beta_bray. The region crosses the section 3 header; the rm() housekeeping line below it is left outside every node.
settings: show_col_types = FALSE, so all column types are guessed by readr from its default row sample rather than declared; alpha_div is bound to the observed (unrarefied) alpha table while the header comment describes alpha_div as standardized to a common sample size; beta_bray is bound to the bay_period_season file, not the consecutive-years file named in the header.
na_behavior: Missing cells become NA by readr's default rules (empty string and NA); nothing here distinguishes a value absent in the source from one that failed type parsing, since a parse failure also yields NA with only a warning. A base absent from latest_data is skipped by list2env and its rename line then aborts with object not found.
notes: Standard filing convention I developed. Used in other code as well.

section: 2a. Diversity-stability (all seasons pooled): fit + display + save
grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season, separately in com_inv and alpha_div
grain_out: one row per major_area x period x season having both stability and diversity present
units_in: I_C invariability index (unitless ratio); richness in species; shannon as q = 1 effective species
units_out: log10 of an invariability index, alongside species count and q = 1 diversity
operation: Joins the alpha diversity columns onto community invariability by major_area, period and season, coerces season to character, takes log10 of I_C, and drops rows missing any of the five analysis columns, producing the single frame every later model uses; the two select statements are absorbed because they only narrow columns. Whether the join keys are unique within alpha_div cannot be determined from this script, and if they are not the left join silently multiplies com_inv rows.
settings: left_join keyed on major_area, period and season; period is a join key but never enters any model; log base 10; drop_na over log_IC, richness, shannon, major_area, season; season coerced to character so its ordering is alphabetical wherever it is later sorted.
na_behavior: com_inv rows with no alpha match receive NA richness and shannon and are then removed by drop_na, so a failed join and a genuinely missing diversity value collapse into the same silent row loss with no count reported anywhere. log10 of a non-positive I_C gives -Inf for zero and NaN for a negative value; drop_na removes the NaN but keeps the -Inf, which then propagates into every model and figure.

section: 2a. Diversity-stability (all seasons pooled): fit + display + save
start_anchor: m_rr <- lmer(log_IC ~ richness + (1 | major_area) + (1 | season), data = df_CS)
end_anchor: m_rr <- lmer(log_IC ~ richness + (1 | major_area) + (1 | season), data = df_CS)
grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season
units_out: fixed-effect slope in log10 invariability per species
operation: Fits log_IC on richness with random intercepts for major_area and season. Because lmerTest is attached, lmer resolves to lmerTest::lmer and the fit carries Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Period is absent from the model, so repeated periods within an area and season are treated as independent replicates.
settings: Random intercepts only, no random slopes; REML = TRUE by default; season enters as a random grouping factor with only the levels surviving drop_na; richness unscaled and untransformed.
na_behavior: df_CS is already complete on these columns, so na.action never fires and no observation count is lost here. A singular or boundary fit still returns a model object with only a warning, and nothing downstream tests for it; an -Inf in log_IC would abort the fit rather than produce an NA coefficient.
notes: I specifically chose random seasonal effect to match with my previous study of occupancy. It is okay.

section: 2a. Diversity-stability (all seasons pooled): fit + display + save
start_anchor: m_sh <- lmer(log_IC ~ shannon  + (1 | major_area) + (1 | season), data = df_CS)
end_anchor: m_sh <- lmer(log_IC ~ shannon  + (1 | major_area) + (1 | season), data = df_CS)
grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season
units_in: log10 invariability; shannon as q = 1 effective species
units_out: fixed-effect slope in log10 invariability per unit of Shannon diversity
operation: Fits log_IC on Shannon diversity with the same random structure as the richness model. It is a separate node from e2.m_rr because the predictor differs, and the two are fitted separately rather than jointly, so the variance shared between richness and Shannon is never partitioned.
settings: Random intercepts for major_area and season, no random slopes; REML = TRUE by default; shannon used on its natural q = 1 scale, not logged; this is the model whose residuals are later fed to the ACF check.
na_behavior: As for the richness model: no NA can arise from the data because drop_na ran upstream, and a singular fit is returned silently rather than flagged.
notes: I specifically chose random seasonal effect to match with my previous study of occupancy. It is okay.

section: 2a. Diversity-stability (all seasons pooled): fit + display + save
units_out: estimate on the model coefficient scale, plus SE, t, df and p
operation: Defines a helper that pulls one named row out of the fixed-effect coefficient table and returns estimate, SE, t, df and p as a one-row tibble; the term is looked up by row name, so the caller must pass the exact predictor string. The trailing bare out is absorbed since it only returns the tibble just built.
settings: df and p are taken only if the columns df and Pr(>|t|) are present, otherwise NA_real_; the term is selected by label rather than by row position, so a change in formula terms changes what is extracted rather than erroring silently.
na_behavior: df and p become NA when the coefficient table lacks those columns, which happens for a plain lme4 fit; that NA is indistinguishable downstream from a model that genuinely produced no p-value. A term_label missing from the table raises a subscript error rather than returning NA, so this failure mode aborts instead of propagating.
notes: Nothing complicated. Just extracting the results.

section: 2a. Diversity-stability (all seasons pooled): fit + display + save
grain_out: one row per model for the fit table, and one row per model x random effect for the SD table
units_out: AIC on the deviance scale, counts of observations and groups, R2 as proportions, SDs in log10 invariability
operation: Defines a helper returning model-level fit statistics together with a tidy table of random-effect standard deviations; the VarCorr reshape and the right-assignment into fitrow are absorbed because they only carry the result forward. Group counts are indexed by the literal names major_area and season, so the helper only works for models with exactly those grouping factors.
settings: R2 marginal and conditional computed only when MuMIn is installed; ngrps looked up by name; residual SD taken from summary sigma; random effect SDs reported as sdcor, which for an intercept-only structure is a standard deviation but for a correlation row would be a correlation.
na_behavior: R2_marginal and R2_conditional are NA when MuMIn is absent and also NA if r.squaredGLMM itself returns NA; the two causes collapse into one NA and nothing records which occurred, so an NA in the saved CSV cannot be read as evidence about the model. A model lacking one of the named grouping factors errors rather than yielding NA.
notes: Nothing complicated. Just extracting the results.

section: 2a. Diversity-stability (all seasons pooled): fit + display + save
grain_out: one row per model x term (fixed effects), one row per model (fit stats), one row per model x random effect (SDs)
units_out: coefficients in log10 invariability per predictor unit; p and q as probabilities
operation: Calls both extraction helpers on the richness and Shannon models, labels each row with its model, stacks them, and adds a BH-adjusted q across the two fixed-effect p-values; the bind_rows and select statements are absorbed since they only stack rows and order columns. The two p-values come from models sharing a response and correlated predictors, so treating them as a family of two tests is a decision a reviewer should check rather than an obvious default.
settings: p.adjust method BH applied to exactly two p-values; model labels logIC ~ richness and logIC ~ shannon carried as strings; output column order fixed by select; the random-effect and fit tables receive no adjustment.
na_behavior: An NA p_value passes through p.adjust as an NA q_value, and since n defaults to the length of the vector, an NA still counts toward the correction denominator, so a failed model quietly makes the surviving q more conservative.

section: 2b. Season-specific slope tests for Shannon and richness (per-season LMMs)
grain_out: one row per season x metric
units_in: log10 invariability and one diversity metric
units_out: slope in log10 invariability per metric unit, with SE, t, df, p and a Wald interval
operation: Defines the per-season fitter: subsets to one season, drops rows missing the response, the predictor or major_area, refuses to fit when fewer than five rows remain or the predictor has zero variance, and otherwise fits log_IC on the predictor with a random intercept for major_area, returning the slope with a Wald confidence interval. Season is now a filter rather than a random effect, so these slopes are not comparable to the pooled model's.
settings: Minimum of 5 rows; sd == 0 guard on the predictor; formula log_IC ~ pred + (1 | major_area); two-sided 0.975 critical value from qt on the Satterthwaite df, falling back to 1.96 when df is not finite; interval is Wald rather than profile or bootstrap; a second drop_na runs inside the function even though df_CS is already complete.
na_behavior: The all-NA row is returned for two distinct reasons, fewer than five rows and zero predictor variance, and the row records only n, so the two causes collapse into one NA row and are not distinguishable downstream except by inspecting n; an NA estimate arising from lmerTest itself would look identical again. Errors inside lmer are not trapped, so a fit that fails outright aborts the whole loop rather than producing an NA row.

section: 2b. Season-specific slope tests for Shannon and richness (per-season LMMs)
grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season
grain_out: one row per season x metric
units_in: log10 invariability and two diversity metrics
units_out: slopes in log10 invariability per metric unit; p and q as probabilities
operation: Runs the per-season fitter over every season present crossed with richness and Shannon, then BH-adjusts across the whole set and sorts by metric and season; seasons_vec and the metrics tibble are absorbed because they only supply the loop with labels. The multiplicity family here is all season x metric tests pooled, whereas the later OLS table adjusts within metric only, so the q columns of the two saved files are not comparable despite both being called BH.
settings: Seasons taken from the data and sorted alphabetically, so the set of tests depends on which seasons survived drop_na; metric labels Shannon (q = 1) and Richness (q = 0); p.adjust method BH over all rows at once; results written to ds_season_slopes_<date>.csv.
na_behavior: All-NA rows returned by the fitter are retained in the table and receive an NA q, while still occupying a slot in the BH denominator; a season that vanished upstream leaves no row and nothing records that it was expected.

section: Combine pooled-season figures into a two-panel figure
start_anchor: fig_DS_richness_all <- ggplot(df_CS, aes(x = richness, y = log_IC)) +
grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season
grain_out: one two-panel figure, one plotted point per input row
units_in: log10 invariability against species count or q = 1 diversity
operation: Draws pooled-season scatterplots of log_IC against richness and against Shannon, each with an OLS fit and confidence band, stacks them with patchwork and writes a TIFF; the labs, theme and tag statements are absorbed as formatting. The plotted line ignores the major_area and season random structure of the models it illustrates, which the comment acknowledges as visual only, so the drawn slope will not match the reported LMM slope.
settings: geom_smooth with method = lm and se = TRUE; point alpha 0.5; na.rm = TRUE on both layers; axis labels assert no rarefaction, which contradicts the file header's description of alpha_div as standardized to a common sample size; panel tags a and b; output 8.5 x 12 cm at 600 dpi, TIFF with LZW compression; the filename carries no date stamp, so a rerun overwrites the previous figure.
na_behavior: na.rm = TRUE removes non-finite points silently and also suppresses the warning that would report how many were removed, so an -Inf log_IC coming from a zero I_C would disappear from both the scatter and the fitted line with no trace in the output.

section: 3. Diversity vs Community Stability - per-season results
grain_out: one row per season x metric
units_in: log10 invariability and one diversity metric
units_out: slope in log10 invariability per metric unit, plus SE, t, p, R2, adjusted R2, n and the F test
operation: Defines a per-season OLS helper; the slope row is selected by predictor name and n is taken from the model frame after listwise deletion. It answers the same per-season question as the per-season LMM helper but without the major_area random intercept, so within-area correlation is ignored here even though the neighbouring table models it.
settings: Formula built by pasting y ~ x; no random effects; both R2 and adjusted R2 returned; F statistic and its two df pulled from summary.
na_behavior: lm applies na.omit, so incomplete rows are dropped and the reported n reflects the reduced sample without saying how many were lost. A zero-variance predictor leaves an NA coefficient row, giving NA slope and SE; a season with too few rows to fit, or a fit that reduces to intercept only, makes the coefficient or fstatistic lookup fail and aborts the run rather than returning NA, so small seasons and unfittable seasons behave differently from one another.

section: 3. Diversity vs Community Stability - per-season results
grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season
grain_out: one row per metric x season
units_in: log10 invariability and two diversity metrics
units_out: slopes in log10 invariability per metric unit; p and q as probabilities; R2 as a proportion
operation: Applies the OLS helper within each season for richness and then for Shannon, stacks the two tables and adds a BH q within each metric across seasons; the metric-labelling mutates and the relocate are absorbed as labelling. These are the same season-by-season relationships already estimated in ds_slope_tests but without the random intercept, so two saved files report different slopes and different q values for the same question.
settings: group_by(season) with group_modify, so seasons are defined by the values present in df_CS; BH applied within metric, that is across four seasons, in contrast to the pooled adjustment used for ds_slope_tests; response fixed at log_IC; written to ds_season_OLS_<date>.csv.
na_behavior: An NA slope from a zero-variance season carries through to NA p and NA q; a season removed upstream by drop_na simply produces no row, and the table gives no signal that a season is missing rather than non-significant.

section: 3. Diversity vs Community Stability - per-season results
grain_out: one row per season x metric
units_in: log10 invariability and one diversity metric
units_out: marginal and conditional R2 as proportions of variance
operation: Defines a helper that refits the per-season mixed model for a given predictor purely to extract marginal and conditional R2; the fitted object is discarded, so this repeats the estimation already done by the per-season slope fitter without returning its coefficients, and the two will disagree if the data passed in differ.
settings: Formula log_IC ~ predictor + (1 | major_area), matching the per-season slope model; MuMIn used only if installed; REML default; no minimum-n or zero-variance guard, unlike the slope fitter.
na_behavior: Both R2 values are NA when MuMIn is absent, indistinguishable in the saved CSV from a case where R2 could not be computed for the fitted model. With no minimum-n guard, a season too small to fit aborts the run instead of returning an NA row, so this helper and the slope fitter fail differently on the same data.

section: 3. Diversity vs Community Stability - per-season results
grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season
grain_out: one row per metric x season
units_in: log10 invariability and two diversity metrics
operation: Runs the R2 helper by season for both metrics and stacks the results into the table saved beside the OLS table; the metric labelling and relocate are absorbed. The R2 here comes from models with a major_area random intercept while the R2 column of the neighbouring OLS table comes from models without one, so the two R2 values for the same season and metric are not on the same footing and should not be compared as written.
settings: group_by(season) with group_modify; same formula as the per-season slope tests; no p-values produced, so no multiplicity adjustment applies; written to ds_season_LMM_R2_<date>.csv.
na_behavior: NA R2 values pass through unchanged and the cause, MuMIn absent versus a computation that returned NA, is not recorded anywhere in the output.

section: Autocorrelation Function (ACF) Check on Model Residuals
end_anchor: acf(res_rr, main = "ACF of Richness-Stability Model Residuals")
grain_out: one autocorrelation per lag, per model
operation: Extracts conditional residuals from the Shannon and richness models and plots their autocorrelation functions. The lag axis is position in the residual vector, which is df_CS row order set by the join over major_area, period and season, not elapsed time, so a lag here steps across areas and seasons unless the frame happens to be ordered as a single time series; whether it is cannot be determined from this script. The line res_sh <- residuals(m_sh) recurs verbatim at the start of the numeric ACF block, the same operation on the same input, so it belongs to this node.
settings: Default lag.max of 10*log10(n); raw conditional residuals rather than Pearson or marginal residuals; no grouping by area or season before computing the ACF; demean = TRUE by default; plots only, nothing is saved.
na_behavior: Residuals of these fits contain no NA because df_CS was made complete upstream, so the default na.action of na.fail never fires; were an NA present, acf would stop rather than return a missing value.

units_out: correlation coefficients and a YES/No flag
operation: Recomputes the Shannon-residual ACF without plotting, forms a white-noise confidence bound, builds a Lag and Autocorrelation table and flags lags above zero whose absolute autocorrelation exceeds the bound; the rounding and data.frame assembly are absorbed as presentation. Each lag is flagged independently with no correction for examining many lags, and the comparison uses the value already rounded to four decimals, so a value at the boundary can flip on rounding.
settings: Bound = 1.96 / sqrt(length(res_sh)), the white-noise approximation that assumes independence under the null and takes no account of lag; lag 0 excluded from flagging; comparison on the absolute rounded autocorrelation; acf defaults otherwise; nothing is written to disk, results are printed only.
na_behavior: No NA arises in normal operation. If an autocorrelation were NA the ifelse would return NA rather than No, so a missing value would appear as an empty Significant cell and read as neither significant nor non-significant.
